analysis.one_liner: Renews farm subsidies and expands food, conservation, and rural aid for five years.
analysis.headline: Congress passed the five-year farm bill over President Bush's veto — the House 316-108 and the Senate 82-13 — making it Public Law 110-234 on May 22, 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: This is the 2008 farm bill, a five-year renewal of farm and food programs. It continues fixed payments and price supports for growers of major commodity crops, sugar, and dairy, and funds conservation, rural development, and disaster programs. It also expands federal nutrition help: the food stamp program was renamed SNAP and given benefit improvements, schools got a fresh fruit and vegetable program, and emergency food programs were extended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households gain through SNAP benefit improvements such as excluding military combat pay from income, raising the minimum standard deduction, removing dependent-care deduction caps, and raising the minimum benefit [S3]. Schoolchildren in low-income schools gain a fresh fruit and vegetable program [S3]. Growers of corn, wheat, cotton, rice, soybeans, peanuts, and sugar gain continued direct payments, counter-cyclical payments, and marketing loans through 2012 [S3]. Beginning and socially disadvantaged farmers gain expanded loan set-asides, and rural communities gain water, broadband, and microenterprise programs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: SNAP (formerly food stamps) benefits improve for working and low-income households: military combat pay is excluded from income, the minimum standard deduction rises and is indexed to inflation, dependent-care deduction caps are removed, retirement and education savings are excluded from asset limits, and the minimum benefit rises to 8% of the maximum [S3].
A new program makes free fresh fruits and vegetables available in elementary schools beginning in the 2008-09 school year, and schools may prefer locally grown foods in purchasing [S3].

Growers of wheat, corn, cotton, rice, soybeans, and peanuts keep fixed direct payments and counter-cyclical payments if prices fall below target levels for crop years 2008-2012, plus nonrecourse marketing loans; a new ACRE option offers revenue-based protection in exchange for a share of those payments [S3].

Producers gain disaster assistance from a new Agricultural Disaster Relief Trust Fund covering crop losses, livestock deaths, and grazing losses, with individual payments capped at $100,000 a year [S3].
Farmers and ranchers gain expanded conservation programs, higher loan limits for beginning farmers, rural broadband and water funding, and organic certification cost-sharing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the bill; the law is partly financed by extending customs user fees and by a temporary 7.125% increase in corporate estimated tax payments due in mid-2012 [S3]. Consumers and food manufacturers bear higher sugar costs, since the law requires sugar marketing allotments be set at levels that keep domestic sugar prices above loan forfeiture levels and limits imports to treaty minimums [S3].

drawbacks.text: Direct payments are made at fixed per-bushel rates (for example, $0.28 per bushel of corn) regardless of market prices, so growers receive checks in good years as well as bad [S3].

The sugar program requires marketing allotments to be set so raw and refined sugar prices exceed loan forfeiture levels, which supports domestic prices above world levels and raises costs for consumers and food makers [S3].

Payment caps remain generous: a person or entity loses benefits only if average nonfarm income exceeds $500,000, and keeps direct payments unless average farm income exceeds $750,000, so large operations remain eligible [S3].
The bill carries tax benefits for narrower interests, including a 15% rate on corporate timber gains and three-year depreciation for race horses [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The nutrition, conservation, and rural development provisions deliver real, broad benefits, and SNAP improvements reached millions of low-income households. But the commodity and sugar titles continue programs whose benefits concentrate on large producers of a handful of crops while the costs spread across taxpayers and consumers, and the income limits leave the largest operations eligible. The bill is a genuine mix: substantial help for ordinary people, purchased in part by entrenching subsidy programs that mostly benefit big operations.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by wide margins, President Bush vetoed it, and both chambers promptly voted to override the veto, making it law.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 231-191 on July 27, 2007, with 212 of 230 Democrats in favor and only 19 of 202 Republicans [S8].
The Senate passed its version 79-14 on December 14, 2007, with 37 of 49 Republicans joining 40 of 49 Democrats [S9].
After a conference committee, the House adopted the conference report 318-106 on May 14, 2008, and the Senate agreed 81-15 on May 15 [S19, S22].
President Bush vetoed the bill on May 21, 2008 [S6].
The House overrode the veto 316-108 and the Senate 82-13 on May 21-22, 2008, and the bill became Public Law 110-234 [S23, S24].
During the conference, motions to instruct conferees to cap direct payments at $40,000 or to reject a permanent disaster program all failed on roll-call votes [S11, S12, S14, S16, S17].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Producers of subsidized commodity crops, sugar processors, and crop insurance companies keep their programs through 2012, while low-income households gain stronger nutrition benefits — with taxpayers funding both.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm subsidy recipients and nutrition beneficiaries

for.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, managed it through House committee markup and floor action, and managed the conference report [S6].

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: Senate conferee on the farm bill
for.what_they_did: Appointed a Senate conferee for the farm bill conference [S6].

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill; both chambers overrode the veto [S6].

against.name: Rep. Jeff Flake
against.what_they_did: Moved to instruct conferees to accept a $40,000 cap on direct payments; the motion failed 157-259, and a similar motion later failed 172-241 [S11, S12].

against.name: Rep. Ron Kind
against.what_they_did: Offered a floor amendment that was defeated in Committee of the Whole, and moved to instruct conferees to insist on payment-limit reforms [S6].

sides.party_line_note: The first House vote split by party (Democrats 212-14 in favor, Republicans 19-177), but the final bill passed both chambers overwhelmingly with large majorities of both parties (House conference report 318-106 with 100 Republicans; Senate 81-15 with 35 Republicans), and the veto overrides were similarly bipartisan [S8, S9, S19, S22, S23, S24].

industries.industry: Producers of program crops (corn, wheat, cotton, rice, soybeans, peanuts)
industries.note: The law locks in fixed direct payments and counter-cyclical payments at set rates through crop year 2012, paid from federal funds whether or not prices are low [S3]. Taxpayers bear the cost while the benefits concentrate on larger operations [S3].

industries.industry: Sugar processors and cane and beet growers
industries.note: The law reauthorizes nonrecourse sugar loans and requires marketing allotments set so domestic sugar prices stay above loan forfeiture levels, limiting domestic marketing and imports [S3]. This props up sugar prices at consumer and food-manufacturer expense.

Federal crop insurance continues with premium subsidies and renegotiated reimbursement of insurers' administrative and operating costs [S3]. Private insurers keep a taxpayer-backed market regardless of farm outcomes.

The law creates a cellulosic biofuel production tax credit, extends the ethanol import tariff to 2011, and funds biorefinery grants and loan guarantees [S3]. The tariff extension protects domestic ethanol producers from cheaper imports.
Dairy price supports continue at set minimums and the milk income loss contract program is extended through 2012 [S3]. Support prices can raise what consumers pay for dairy products.
The law sets a 15% tax rate on corporate timber gains and eases REIT rules for timber income [S3]. This is a targeted tax benefit for timber owners.

Sugar marketing allotments and import limits keep domestic sugar prices above forfeiture levels, raising input costs for food manufacturers and, ultimately, consumers [S3]. Their interest in cheaper sugar runs alongside ordinary people's.
